claims.text: The Ni-based superalloy components are susceptible to hot cracking during traditional fusion-welding repair.
Localized laser shock peening will create a near-surface compressive residual-stress layer.
Localized laser shock peening will refine the near-surface microstructure.
Localized laser shock peening will increase near-surface dislocation density.
Laser energy densities of 5–10 GW/cm² constitute a suitable range for the proposed localized treatment.
High-intensity laser pulses generate rapid shock waves that plastically deform the surface.
The induced compressive stress and refined microstructure will delay crack initiation and propagation under aggressive service conditions.
Localized laser shock peening will delay surface-defect initiation.
Localized laser shock peening will reduce hot-cracking risk relative to traditional fusion-welding repair.
The treated surface will have greater hardness than fusion-weld-repaired and untreated surfaces.
The treated surface will have greater wear resistance than fusion-weld-repaired and untreated surfaces.
The treated surface will have greater corrosion resistance than fusion-weld-repaired and untreated surfaces.
Traditional fusion-weld repairs and untreated surfaces both have inferior surface mechanical properties and greater hot-cracking susceptibility than laser-shock-peened surfaces.
Treatment effectiveness depends on precise control of laser energy density and treatment uniformity.
The proposed benefits may not transfer to other material systems without process modification.
Prior literature supports laser shock peening for improving fatigue and crack resistance.
Over-peening can induce microcracking or surface degradation.
